headline: Three hours at the Dispatch Box, and an exit by the Chiltern Hundreds

body: The House came back on Tuesday 1 September to a Prime Minister it had never questioned and a former Prime Minister it was about to lose. Andy Burnham had been in office for 43 days — “during which,” Kemi Badenoch told him, “I have learned how he puts the milk in his tea and exactly what he thinks about pork scratchings, but I have not had the pleasure of asking him any questions. We are all grateful that he has finally found time to come to Parliament to answer some.” The Speaker, before calling him, had a word for those who had asked why he said nothing over the recess: “it is within the rules, which I do not make.” The statement began at 3.39 pm and the last answer was given at 6.49 pm; the Prime Minister replied 118 times, and by the Leader of the Opposition’s count the next day it was “125 questions” — “Three hours!” — a record Mr Burnham claimed for himself at Prime Minister’s Questions as “the longest statement in modern history.” Its first passage was a farewell: “as he stands down from this place, I want to pay tribute to my right hon. and learned Friend the Member for Holborn and St Pancras (Keir Starmer). He has given this country a lifetime of public service.” That evening the Treasury published the sentence by which a Member of Parliament leaves: “The Chancellor of the Exchequer has this day appointed Sir Keir Starmer to be Steward and Bailiff of the Three Hundreds of Chiltern.” The Commons register closed his membership the same day — “Resignation (Chiltern)” — and now holds 649 names. Holborn and St Pancras, which he won in 2024 by 11,572 votes, awaits a writ that neither sitting day moved.

The statement was a diagnosis, and the diagnosis was of forty years. “From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns. Political power was centralised, economic power privatised and the country deindustrialised.” Sir Iain Duncan Smith asked, “Who wrote this?” The water industry was “a leaking monument to that approach”; No. 10 North, six weeks old, would oversee “the rewiring of the British state”; Cornwall was offered a devolution deal “with or without an elected mayor,” and “all parts of England without devolved power” the same; summer small-boat arrivals had “halved on last year”; and the House was asked to help end imprisonment for public protection sentences, “a now abolished policy, but one which to this day keeps people behind bars despite having already served more than their sentences.” Ed Davey asked for the national commission on electoral reform that “over 170 Members” have signed, and did not get it. Mr Burnham’s riposte to the Opposition was arithmetic: “In six days, this Government will have outlived the Truss Government.” On Wednesday the Speaker admired the Prime Minister’s detailed answers and worried he was “not going to get through the list.” Mrs Badenoch asked what, exactly, he had cut to pay for his summer — “tax is the simple answer,” he said, and digital ID “is not a priority for me or for this Government” — and whether he would rule out tax rises; he would not write the Budget at the Dispatch Box. He reminded her that her new shadow Chancellor “helped to write the Truss mini-Budget,” recalled her verdict that Liz Truss was “100% right,” and offered the House his own: “God help us!” Jack Rankin asked him to state the fiscal rules and got one sentence: “No borrowing to fund day-to-day spending, debt falling as a percentage of GDP by the end of the Parliament, and yes, we will.”

Two more statements followed the Prime Minister’s on Tuesday night, and a third on Wednesday. The Lord Chancellor, Alex Norris, confirmed that early release under the Sentencing Act will now exclude “all unlawful killing offences — including death by dangerous or drink-driving, causing or allowing the death of a child, and manslaughter — as well as indecent assault,” that more than £110 million is being brought forward for prison places, that foreign offenders on determinate sentences will from next year be removed “immediately after sentencing,” and that legislation will end IPP sentences “once and for all, by the end of this Parliament” — more than 2,000 people remain on them, and of those never released 99 per cent are past their tariff. Nick Timothy called it “the Government’s fifth early release policy in just six weeks”; a written answer on Wednesday moved the first tranche of releases from 2 September to 1 October. At 8.07 pm Shabana Mahmood recounted the facts of 22 August: at 3.39 in the morning a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way down the A66 collided with a marked Cleveland police car, killing PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough, 37 and 38, and the five young men in the Passat; 27 arrests have followed, and the force gets £2 million more. On Wednesday Louise Haigh, the first woman to be First Secretary of State “since the late, great Barbara Castle,” described the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet — No. 10 North “fully funded from existing Cabinet Office budgets,” at Heron House in Manchester — and the summer’s fires: 47 wildfires burning on 13 August, close to 12,000 999 calls in a single day, a national emergency alert on 14 August, and calls down 42 per cent within 48 hours. Alex Burghart, noting that “rewiring the state” was his own leader’s phrase from 2024, saw in the new OneGov Delivery Agency “a massive new quango,” and in the Treasury’s survival the empire striking back.

The week’s four divisions came in fifty-five minutes on Wednesday evening, all on the Representation of the People Bill, and the Government won all four. The Conservatives’ new clause 65, for an independent review of how overseas electors register and vote, fell 166 to 346 with the Liberal Democrats in the Aye lobby; their new clause 67, to make it an offence to publish campaign material “in a foreign language” — “We must put a stop to election literature in foreign languages once and for all,” said Katie Lam — fell 105 to 410 with the Liberal Democrats against it; and the Liberal Democrats’ new clause 88, for a Royal Commission on a cap on political donations, fell 85 to 427 with the Conservatives against it. The clause 170 Members wanted, a national commission on electoral reform, was out of scope — “frankly ridiculous,” said Ellie Chowns, “in a Bill about elections called the Representation of the People Bill.” The Government’s own new clauses propose a ban on political donations in cryptoassets, retrospective to 25 March 2026. Two people were new to their places: Florence Eshalomi, whose resignation as Chair of the Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee the Speaker had announced on Tuesday, moved the clauses as Minister; Katie Lam, opposite her, paid tribute to “my predecessor,” Sir James Cleverly, who had tabled 457 written questions to the department on the Friday and was no longer shadowing it by the Wednesday. At 7.59 pm the Bill passed its Third Reading by 411 votes to 102 — Labour, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National Party, the Greens and Plaid Cymru in the Aye lobby, the Conservatives and Reform UK in the No — and goes to the Lords. On Tuesday the House agreed the Ways and Means resolution for a Sovereign Grant Bill that cuts the grant from £137.9 million to £99.9 million in 2027-28, the Buckingham Palace reservicing being nearly done; the Bill was presented that night. In the Lords the Hillsborough law — the Public Office (Accountability) Bill — had its second reading on Tuesday in a debate running to nearly 50,000 words; the Social Housing Bill passed its third reading and reached the Commons; the Armed Forces Bill entered committee. The Lord Speaker recorded the retirement of Lord Jopling and the deaths of Lord Horam and Lord Snape.

Beneath all this the written record did something it has not done in the life of this digest: 6,683 questions were tabled in the window, and 6,153 of them carry the same date, Friday 28 August, when the House was still four days from meeting — more in a day than any full sitting week here has recorded. Two hundred and sixty-five Members tabled that Friday; 3,686 of the week’s questions are Conservative, 1,304 Labour, 850 Liberal Democrat. Ben Obese-Jecty, the Member for Huntingdon, put 703 and is this issue’s feature; Mike Wood, a shadow Cabinet Office minister, put 654, all on the Friday and 309 of them to the Cabinet Office, eighteen under the heading “Lord Mandelson”; James McMurdock, the 22 July feature, put 491 and received on Wednesday the reply that the Department “does not hold a single formal timeline of events” leading to the Basildon notice; Charlie Dewhirst put near-identical questions on communications staff and unpaid work to twenty-two departments, 340 in all. Twelve questions are headed “No 10 North,” among them Gregory Stafford’s “whether No.10 North will pay rent or any other charge for its occupation of space at GCHQ’s Heron House” — Louise Haigh, on Wednesday, noted “the sheer quantity of parliamentary questions and freedom of information requests that have come in over the summer.” The wry note belongs to Helen Morgan, who on 8 July asked when three earlier questions would be answered and was told, on 1 September, to see the answers given by two ministers the reply itself calls “former.” The grave one belongs to Apsana Begum, told that the rise in recorded postpartum haemorrhage “may be influenced by” better reporting — 92 per cent of trusts now in the data, against 30 per cent in 2020 — “in addition to any rise in clinical incidence.” Tom Gordon asked the Work and Pensions Secretary what he was doing to encourage employers to adopt workplace suicide-prevention standards and received two sentences on whose responsibility the strategy is. Stella Creasy asked when the Fulford review of national security vetting will be published: a summary, “in due course.” The register holds 649.

feature.title: Seven hundred and three questions from Huntingdon
feature.status: written questions tabled 28 Aug – 1 Sep; 449 to the Ministry of Defence, 76 to the Ministry of Justice, 37 to the Home Office; one answered by 2 Sep
feature.summary: Ben Obese-Jecty holds no front-bench post. On Friday 28 August, four days before the House met, the Conservative Member for Huntingdon tabled 684 written questions, and on the Tuesday he added nineteen — 703 in all, 449 of them to the Ministry of Defence, the largest file from one Member this digest has seen. It is not a broadside; it is an audit. Forty-four questions cite the 2025 Strategic Defence Review by recommendation number; twenty-two cite the Ministry’s annual report and accounts; seventeen work through the “UK armed forces equipment and formations 2026” statistics published on 20 August, asking after each item the fleet is smaller by — the one BV-206, the two quad bikes, the 41 Wolfhounds, the one General Support Bridge. Others go row by row through the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s major-projects tables: E-7 Wedgetail, the Multi Role Strike Ship, Armoured Cavalry 2025, the Submarine Dismantling Project and its whole-life cost. Under “Defence: Procurement” alone there are forty-four; under “Armoured Fighting Vehicles” eighteen; under “Guided Weapons” and “Unmanned Air Systems” ten each; and a second front at the Ministry of Justice, eleven on prison accommodation, in the week the Lord Chancellor promised places brought forward. By Wednesday night one had been answered. The Order Paper is not built to be read as a spreadsheet, but nothing in the rules stops a Member using it as one, and the answers, when they come, will be the fullest public reconciliation of the Defence Investment Plan against the equipment that actually exists.
questions: Ben Obese-Jecty (Conservative, Huntingdon) — 703 questions in two tabling days, 684 of them on Friday 28 August: the Strategic Defence Review recommendation by recommendation, the equipment and formations statistics vehicle by vehicle, and the major-projects tables row by row.
The Ministry of Defence takes 449 of them, under headings from “Defence: Procurement” (44) and “Armoured Fighting Vehicles” (18) to “Minesweepers,” “Nuclear Weapons” and “Type 31 Frigates.”
A second front at the Ministry of Justice — 76 questions, eleven of them on prison accommodation — in the week the Lord Chancellor brought forward more than £110 million for prison places.

qa.heading: Prisoners' Release
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Justice, how many offenders will be released (a) on 2 September 2026 and (b) at each of the following monthly release points under the Sentencing Act 2026 by offence including rape, child grooming, sexual assault, manslaughter, causing death by dangerous driving and child cruelty.
qa.answer: This Government inherited a prisons system days from collapse. We had no choice but to take decisive action to stop our prisons overflowing and keep the public safe. Our landmark Sentencing Act 2026 will now deliver a more sustainable solution to the prison capacity crisis we inherited, including through the progression model which will help ensure there are always enough places for the courts to be able to send people to custody in order to keep the public safe. The progression model amends release points for offenders serving standard determinate sentences. That is why we have taken tough decisions to stop prisons running out of space while keeping the public safe. But we have also listened to victims and acted on their concerns. Any unlawful killing offence such as manslaughter, death by dangerous driving, as well as further historic child sex offences, will now be excluded, on top of rape and serious child sex offences. A full list of exclusions can be found here: Sentencing Act 2026 offence exclusions - GOV.UK These exclusions are in addition to the existing exclusion of over 18,000 offenders serving the most more serious sentences. The date from which the progression model will apply, and the date of the first tranche of releases, has changed. The first tranche of releases will no longer take place on 2 September 2026 as previously planned, but on 1 October 2026.

qa.heading: Postpartum Haemorrhage
qa.department: Department of Health and Social Care
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what steps his Department is taking to address rates of postpartum haemorrhage in England.
qa.answer: NHS England is working to improve the timely clinical response to obstetric haemorrhage through the Maternal Care Bundle, which aims to improve the management of haemorrhage through timely identification, escalation, and response to obstetric bleeding, along with ongoing, multidisciplinary review and learning. Significant improvements in data coverage and data quality over recent years mean that in September 2025, 92% of National Health Service trusts were included in the analysis of Maternity Services Data Set birth and postpartum haemorrhage information, compared with 30% in September 2020. The referenced increase in postpartum haemorrhage rates may be influenced by this improvement in reporting in addition to any rise in clinical incidence.

qa.heading: Department of Health and Social Care: Written Questions
qa.department: Department of Health and Social Care
qa.question: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, hen he plans to respond to Question 4447, 10962 and 15024 tabled by the hon. Member for North Shropshire on 29 May, 17 June and 1 July 2026.
qa.answer: I refer the hon. Member to: the answer my hon. Friend, the former Minister of State for Care, gave on 8 July 2026 to Question 4447; the answer my hon. Friend, the former Parliamentary Under-secretary of State for Health Innovation and Safety, gave on 12 July 2026 to Question 10962; and the answer my hon. Friend, the Minister of State for Health, gave on 19 August 2026 to Question 15024.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Third Reading

votes.blurb: The Bill through the Commons at 7.59 pm, 411 to 102 — Labour, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National Party, the Greens and Plaid Cymru for; the Conservatives and Reform UK against. Emma Foody and Jade Botterill had told the Noes three times that evening; this time they told the Ayes.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Report stage: New Clause 67

votes.blurb: The sharpest of the four. New clause 67 would have made it an offence to publish campaign material “in a foreign language” during an election. “We must put a stop to election literature in foreign languages once and for all,” said Katie Lam. The Liberal Democrats voted with the Government; defeated 105 to 410.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 88

votes.blurb: The Liberal Democrats’ new clause 88, for a Royal Commission on a cap on political donations and on the reach of spending limits, after a summer Joe Powell said had barely passed a day “without another political funding scandal on the front pages.” The Conservatives voted with the Government; defeated 85 to 427.

row.title: Representation of the People Bill: Report Stage: New Clause 65

votes.blurb: The first division of the new term, at 7.04 pm. The Conservatives’ new clause 65, for an independent review of how overseas electors register and vote, drew the Liberal Democrats into the Aye lobby and still fell, 166 to 346.

bills.blurb: Report stage and Third Reading on 2 September, and the week’s only divisions — three Opposition new clauses defeated in half an hour, then the Bill read the third time by 411 votes to 102 at 7.59 pm. The Government’s own new clauses propose a retrospective ban on donations in cryptoassets from 25 March 2026. It goes to the Lords.

Ways and Means resolution agreed on 1 September and the Bill presented that night (Bill 137). It cuts the Sovereign Grant from £137.9 million to £99.9 million in 2027-28, the Buckingham Palace reservicing programme being nearly complete. Second reading is promised later this month.

The Hillsborough law had its second reading in the Lords on 1 September, a debate running to nearly 50,000 words, with Baroness May of Maidenhead, Baroness Manningham-Buller and Lord Blunkett among the speakers.
Through the Lords: third reading on 1 September, first reading in the Commons on 2 September. The Bill that spent the recess in the unelected House now belongs to the elected one.
The five-yearly renewal of the Armed Forces Act began its Lords committee stage on 2 September, the first day of what is usually several.

overview.headline: Burnham answers for three hours and Starmer leaves the House
overview.intro: The House of Commons returned on Tuesday 1 September. Andy Burnham had been Prime Minister for forty-three days and had never been questioned in the House. He made a statement on the direction of his Government and answered Members of Parliament for three hours and ten minutes. The Official Report records 118 replies. Kemi Badenoch counted 125 questions. He told the House that the country took a series of wrong turns from the 1980s, offered every part of England without devolved power a devolution deal with or without a mayor, and asked for help to end imprisonment for public protection sentences. He opened with a tribute to Sir Keir Starmer, who was standing down. That evening the Chancellor appointed Sir Keir Steward and Bailiff of the Three Hundreds of Chiltern, which is the device by which a Member of Parliament leaves. The Commons now has 649 members and Holborn and St Pancras will need a by-election. The rest of the week brought three more ministerial statements, the first Prime Minister's Questions of the new Government, four votes on the Representation of the People Bill and 6,683 written questions.

brief.title: The Prime Minister's statement on the direction of government
brief.note: Andy Burnham spoke from 3.39 pm and gave his last answer at 6.49 pm. He paid tribute to Sir Keir Starmer as he stands down from the House. He said that from the 1980s the country took a series of wrong turns, with political power centralised, economic power privatised and the country deindustrialised. Sir Iain Duncan Smith asked who wrote it. He offered Cornwall a devolution deal with or without an elected mayor and extended the offer to all parts of England without devolved power. He said summer small boat arrivals had halved on last year. He told the Opposition that in six days his Government would have outlived the Truss Government.

brief.title: Criminal justice reform
brief.note: The Lord Chancellor, Alex Norris, said early release under the Sentencing Act will now exclude all unlawful killing offences, including death by dangerous or drink driving and manslaughter, as well as indecent assault. More than £110 million is being brought forward for prison places. Legislation will end imprisonment for public protection sentences by the end of this Parliament. Nick Timothy called it the fifth early release policy in six weeks. A written answer on Wednesday moved the first releases from 2 September to 1 October.

brief.title: Policing in Cleveland
brief.note: Shabana Mahmood told the House that at 3.39 in the morning of 22 August a car travelling the wrong way down the A66 hit a marked Cleveland police vehicle. PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough died, as did the five young men in the car. They were thirty-seven and thirty-eight. There have been twenty-seven arrests in a wider investigation into serious and organised crime. The force will receive an extra £2 million.

brief.title: Foreign Office questions and the Chagos treaty
brief.note: Luke Evans asked whether the department has budgeted for future spending on the treaty with Mauritius over the Chagos archipelago, and asked the minister to confirm that the deal is dead. Uma Kumaran said the funding will come from the existing spending review settlements for the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence, and gave no figure. Wendy Morton quoted the Government's own words from April, that the treaty had become impossible to agree at political level after the United States withdrew support.

brief.title: Prime Minister's Questions, then the First Secretary
brief.note: Kemi Badenoch asked what the Prime Minister had cut to pay for his summer promises. He said tax was the simple answer and that digital identity cards are not a priority. He would not rule out tax rises and would not write the Budget at the Dispatch Box. Asked to state the fiscal rules he gave one sentence, no borrowing for day to day spending and debt falling as a share of the economy by the end of the Parliament. Louise Haigh then described the new Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

brief.title: Representation of the People Bill
brief.note: The week's four votes were all on this Bill and the Government won all four. Conservative clauses on overseas electors and on campaign material in foreign languages both fell, as did a Liberal Democrat clause for a Royal Commission on a cap on political donations. The Government's own clauses propose a ban on donations in cryptoassets. Florence Eshalomi answered as the new minister and Katie Lam spoke as the new shadow. The Bill then passed its Third Reading by 411 votes to 102, with the Conservatives and Reform UK voting against, and goes to the House of Lords.
